title: Coauthorship integrity: Reconceptualising assessment validity for the age of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Mohsen Ebrahimzadeh; Antonette Shibani; Simon Buckingham Shum
ft_reason: University context (non-proctored writing assessment); assessment validity and academic integrity are the primary focus; GenAI/LLM-based AI Viva; peer-reviewed journal article; 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Conceptual/framework paper (Coauthorship Integrity as a new source of validity evidence) plus proof-of-concept design of an LLM 'AI Viva' prototype and a preliminary expert evaluation (think-aloud, 0-10 ratings and semi-structured interviews)
discipline: Not discipline-specific (writing assessment generally); expert evaluators from linguistics, education, urban studies, futures studies and museology
level: Higher education (general); evaluation used academic staff, not students
sample: 8 expert educators at UTS (3 subject-matter experts, 5 also assessment experts; teaching experience M = 10.5 years, SD = 6.07), each evaluating the prototype on a journal paper they brought (self-authored in 7 of 8 cases); sessions about 90 min (two about 160 min)
genai_tools: GPT-4-1106 via the Microsoft Azure Playground Assistant (university tenant); system prompt of about 29,000 words defining 30 item variants

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that GenAI use in non-proctored writing threatens all five AERA/APA/NCME sources of validity evidence, and propose Coauthorship Integrity (whether the student can account for and defend the ideas in a possibly AI-coauthored text) as an additional, foundational source of validity evidence.

The AI Viva prototype generates comprehension items (multiple-choice, matching, true/false, cloze and open-ended) from the submitter's own text across all six levels of Bloom's revised taxonomy, scores responses, gives a structured feedback report and invites follow-up dialogue.

Experts rated open-ended items higher for checking comprehension (means 8.38-9.00 for Remember to Analyze and Create levels) than recognition items such as multiple-choice (6.38) and cloze (6.25); perceived difficulty rose broadly from Remember to Create.

Scoring accuracy and feedback quality were rated highly for items 1-8 (means about 8.1-9.6), and in post-viva dialogue the agent held its score of 0 for a deliberately irrelevant answer when the expert contested it; Evaluate- and Create-level answers were not scored because of time limits.
The authors position the AI Viva as formative only at this stage; summative use would require assessment-security measures, and preventing AI-on-AI cheating remains unresolved.

dimensions.authenticity: Notes that shifting to proctored exams in response to GenAI shrinks assessment variety and authenticity (Sec 2.5).
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes verifying students' epistemic ownership of their writing through LLM-generated, text-specific comprehension questions and dialogue (Sec 3-5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Reframes integrity from a provenance problem to a validity problem; acknowledges that summative use would need identity verification and lockdown, and that AI-on-AI cheating is unresolved (Sec 2, Sec 8.3, Sec 8.6).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Items are mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy levels, but alignment to course learning outcomes is not tested (Sec 5.3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Accepts human/AI coauthorship as pervasive and locates misconduct in a lack of accountability for the work rather than AI use itself (Sec 1, Sec 9).
dimensions.scalability: Argues AI Vivas could deliver viva-like evidence at scale, unlike labour-intensive human vivas; scale is not demonstrated (Sec 3, Sec 9).
dimensions.workload: Human vivas and interactive orals are described as resource- and time-intensive for large cohorts, motivating automation (Sec 3).
dimensions.feasibility: Preliminary expert evaluation supports technical feasibility, but only with high-quality expert texts and a researcher driving a basic chat interface (Sec 6.2, Sec 8.6).
dimensions.process_visibility: The dialogic mode is presented as a way to elicit response-process evidence about students' reasoning (Sec 8.1.3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: A text-based rather than spoken viva was chosen partly because verbal formats can disadvantage students with language or accessibility needs (Sec 4).

author_recommendations: Adopt Coauthorship Integrity as an additional source of validity evidence for non-proctored assessment (not tested).
Use AI Vivas formatively to build students' metacognitive awareness of how they use GenAI (preliminary expert evaluation only; not tested with students).
Treat any summative use with great caution and add security measures such as identity verification and locked-down or invigilated conditions (not tested).
Ground the LLM in quality-assured sources to avoid reinforcing misconceptions in the student's text (not tested).
Develop 'AI Viva Analytics' to identify cohort misconceptions under clear privacy governance (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge: small expert sample (n = 8) using high-quality, mostly self-authored texts, which is an optimal case and may inflate performance; no testing with students or student texts; Evaluate/Create items not scored; text-only prototype cannot handle multimodal or mathematical content and does not simulate oral social dynamics; risk of reinforcing misconceptions in the source text; unresolved AI-on-AI cheating for summative use (Sec 8.6). In addition, the qualitative analysis procedure for interviews is not described, and ratings are descriptive only.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear aims and RQs; conceptual argument grounded in the AERA et al. (2014) Standards; expert sample and procedure described (Table 1, Sec 6); ratings and dialogue examples support the modest proof-of-concept claims; explicit limitations section. Evidence is preliminary and expert-only, so it does not show effects on students.

title: AI in action: Changes to student perceptions when using generative artificial intelligence for the creation of a multimedia project-based assessment
authors: Kellie A. Charles; Arsalan Yousuf; Han Chow Chua; Slade T. Matthews; Joanna Harnett; Tina Hinton
ft_reason: Final-year undergraduate capstone unit; pilots an AI-permitted authentic group multimedia assessment and examines AI use and assessment integrity (substantial focus); GenAI; peer-reviewed journal; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (constructivist paradigm) of one unit; abductive thematic analysis of routinely collected LMS data (pre-semester Padlet posts and group project logbooks) using Messeri and Crockett's four AI personas; frequencies of personas reported
discipline: Pharmacology (capstone interdisciplinary research unit PCOL3888, Bachelor of Science)
sample: 40 enrolled students contributed Padlet posts (4355 words; 71 persona descriptions); 2 withdrew, leaving 38 students in 5 project groups of 7-8; 14 AI use cases from the logbooks of 4 groups (one group reported no AI use); semester 2, 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT (most used, by four groups), OpenAI DALL-E 3, TikTok AI voice tool

key_findings.finding: AI use was permitted in all assessments except reflections, provided students acknowledged the tools and described their prompts and how outputs were integrated; the group logbook recorded roles, meetings, decisions and AI use.
Before the projects, students mostly saw AI in a tutor-like Arbiter role (49%), then Oracle (41%) and Quant (10%); 70% described two or more roles and none described AI as a Surrogate.

Actual use was low to moderate and confined mainly to idea generation (Oracle, 12 of 14 cases, 86%) and data analysis (Quant, 2 cases, 14%); no group used AI as an Arbiter or to write text for the final submission.

All projects reached distinction or above (over 85%) and were submitted with AI acknowledgements, but only one group fully documented prompts and outputs with evidence of evaluative judgement; two groups did so only partially.

The authors attribute the gap between perceived and actual use to student uncertainty, including conflicting messages from other units equating AI use with plagiarism, and call for assessing the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs.

dimensions.authenticity: The group multimedia education-campaign project was designed on authentic and sustainable assessment principles to mirror research and professional roles (Sec 1, Sec 2.1, Sec 4).
dimensions.integrity_security: Authors argue that clear guidance on assessing AI-supported process is needed to protect assessment integrity, and that bans, detectors or full return to invigilated tasks are not feasible for large science units (Abstract, Sec 4).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Unit learning outcomes are mapped to university graduate qualities, including digital literacy (Appendix 1, Table 2).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI was openly encouraged with acknowledgement, yet students used it sparingly and mainly for brainstorming, suggesting uncertainty about appropriate use (Sec 3.3, Sec 4).
dimensions.feasibility: Supervisors had limited AI know-how, so no guidance on specific tools or teaching on how to use them was given (Sec 2.1).
dimensions.process_visibility: Logbooks with AI-use descriptions made the process visible, but documentation quality varied, with only one group fully detailing inputs, outputs and judgements (Sec 2.3.2, Sec 3.3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes that students more confident in academic writing, including native speakers, may be less likely to use AI (Sec 4).

author_recommendations: Pilot assessments that explicitly acknowledge and incorporate AI use (not tested beyond this single pilot).
Assess the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs, not just the product (not tested).
Provide clear guidance to educators and students on assessing AI-supported learning (not tested).
Expand professional development in AI literacy for educators and share exemplars of AI integration (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge: a small cohort of final-year science students in one specialised unit; few AI use cases; findings may reflect the early stage of AI tools in late 2023 (Sec 4.1). Also noted: the two withdrawn students' anonymous Padlet posts could not be removed; researchers taught the unit (reflexivity statement, Sec 2.6); no explicit AI guidance was given to students.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear aims; case study design with a theory-based coding framework, multiple coders and a reflexivity statement; sample and data sources well described; findings are supported by frequencies and use-case table; limitations section present. Small single-unit, non-computing sample limits transfer.

title: The impact of generative AI on academic integrity of authentic assessments within a higher education context
authors: Alexander Kofinas; Crystal Han‐Huei Tsay; David Pike
ft_reason: Two UK universities (undergraduate business programmes); academic integrity of authentic assessments and GenAI detection in marking is the primary focus; GenAI (ChatGPT 3.5); peer-reviewed BJET article; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Exploratory two-phase within-subjects experiment (blind marking of human-authored, GenAI-modified and GenAI-generated scripts, then pair reconciliation) with descriptive statistics, followed by semi-structured interviews analysed thematically (mixed methods)
discipline: Business studies (BSc Business Management; BA Business Purchasing and Supply Chain Management)
sample: 8 academic markers in 4 pairs (3-15 years HE experience); per institution 21 writing samples (three levels, each with 3 original student scripts at three grade bands, 3 GenAI-modified versions and 1 GenAI-generated script); six assessments mapped for authenticity using Hobbins et al. (2022) and Kaider et al. (2017); four interviews of about 2 hours

key_findings.finding: Pairs' accuracy in identifying which scripts involved GenAI ranged from 33.3% (7 of 21) to 85.7% (18 of 21); the most accurate pair included the module leader, who relied on familiarity with students' writing styles.
Markers' suspicion produced six false positives on original student work and seven false negatives on GenAI-modified or GenAI-generated work.

GenAI modification raised marks mainly in the 50-59 band (9 of 12 cases, by 2-8 points), while originally first-class scripts were often marked down, suggesting markers penalised work they saw as too perfect.
Six GenAI-generated scripts, each produced in 90 minutes or less by researchers acting as a 'mischievous' student, received upper-second marks (55-70).
Differences in assessment authenticity made very little difference to detecting GenAI use, so the authors conclude that authentic assessment alone is not a safeguard.

dimensions.authenticity: Assessments ranging from low to moderate/high authenticity were all easily reproduced or modified with GenAI; more authentic tasks are also more complex and time-consuming to run (Methodology, Tables 1-2; Discussion).
dimensions.capability_verification: Argues that written, asynchronous outputs are no longer reliable indicators of learning and that performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments are needed (Conclusions).
dimensions.integrity_security: Markers could not reliably detect GenAI input, and suspicion led to both false positives and false negatives (Results, Tables 4-5).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Discusses constructive alignment and backwash as the basis for assessment design (Literature review).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Suggests GenAI could be used intentionally in assessment, for example to simulate professional environments or give iterative feedback (not tested) (Conclusions).
dimensions.scalability: Notes that highly authentic assessments are harder to manage with high student volumes (Discussion).
dimensions.workload: Notes that guidance requiring orals for every high AI-detection score would make marking far more onerous (Discussion).
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends shifting from assessing outputs to assessing process and workplace relevance (Practitioner notes; Conclusions).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Honest students may be penalised on suspicion alone, which raises a fairness concern (Results).

author_recommendations: Give more critical attention to assessment design rather than relying on authenticity alone (not tested).
Shift towards performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments such as interactive orals and role-plays (not tested).
Assess process and socially situated knowledge application rather than written outputs (not tested).
Use GenAI intentionally in assessment design, for example to simulate professional scenarios (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge the experiment was exploratory with a small sample (Conclusions), and that markers' detection cues (e.g. disjointedness due to ChatGPT 3.5 limits) may not hold for newer models (Discussion). Also noted: convenience sampling at the authors' own institutions; markers knew some scripts involved GenAI, which may have biased marking; no third marker; descriptive statistics only; the RQ3 conclusion is not broken down by authenticity level in the tables.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear RQs, appropriate exploratory design and well-described sample and materials. q4 Unclear because conclusions (especially RQ3 on authenticity) rest on descriptive counts from 8 markers without a per-authenticity analysis. Limitations are acknowledged only briefly.

title: Adapting to AI: Innovative Approaches for Homework in Computer Science Education
ft_reason: Undergraduate CS (introductory programming) context; homework/assignment design for integrity under AI tools is the primary focus; GenAI; FIE 2025 innovative practice work-in-progress paper (peer-reviewed conference); 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5, although the evidence base is thin.
study_design: Innovative practice work-in-progress / experience report: informal comparison of ChatGPT-4o solutions and instructor or textbook-author solutions for two introductory Python questions, followed by assignment-design recommendations
level: Undergraduate (introductory programming; students with little or no prior experience)
sample: Two programming questions (one elementary, one intermediate) adapted from a Python textbook; no student participants or data
genai_tools: ChatGPT-4o (used for comparison); ChatGPT, Stable Diffusion, Meta Llama 3, Mistral AI and GPT-4o listed as examples

key_findings.finding: For both questions, the ChatGPT-4o and instructor solutions shared core features (correct output, appropriate variable names, input handling, formatted output, comments).

The authors judge the differences distinct enough to tell human from AI code: AI solutions were more robust, followed standard practice and used concepts beyond what had been taught, whereas novice code is expected to stick to taught concepts. They also note that students can prompt AI to simplify code.
They recommend making homework depend on highly specific domain knowledge from lectures (e.g. edge cases discussed only in class) so that AI tools struggle to solve it.
They also recommend ambiguous, open-ended requirements that need student choices and written justifications, so that the task cannot simply be pasted into an AI tool.
The conclusion acknowledges that detecting AI-generated code remains challenging and often impractical.

dimensions.authenticity: Example tasks draw on realistic scenarios (a customer-data GUI with messy names and addresses; a degree-progress tracker) (Sec 7-8).
dimensions.capability_verification: Tasks requiring students to justify their own choices are proposed to show student rather than AI work (not tested) (Sec 8).
dimensions.integrity_security: Motivated by integrity concerns; argues any homework can be passed to an AI tool, and that style-based detection is limited (Sec 1, Sec 5, Sec 11).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Assignments should still target the intended skills while being harder to solve with AI (Sec 6).

author_recommendations: Test assignments in AI tools to understand the responses they generate (not tested).
Embed lecture-specific, less commonly known details in homework (not tested).
Use ambiguous, open-ended requirements and ask students to justify their choices (not tested).
Build instructor awareness of what AI-generated code looks like, while recognising detection limits (not tested).
limitations: No limitations section. The comparison uses only two questions and one AI tool, with no student data; recommendations are not evaluated; section numbering jumps from 8 to 11, suggesting a truncated work-in-progress paper. The running header says SIGCSE TS 2025 while the footer and DOI give FIE 2025.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Aim is clear, but the method is an informal two-item comparison; the recommendations (Sec 7-8) are not derived from or tested against data; no limitations section beyond a brief comment on detection limits.

title: Process over Product: A Real-Time, Big Data Approach to Plagiarism Detection via Activity Logs
authors: B S Anurag Rao; Shreya Gurram; Justin Carvalho; Adhithya P S; Animesh Giri
ft_reason: University CS setting (sophomore students; hackathon and in-class assignment); academic integrity (plagiarism detection, including AI-generated code) is the primary focus; GenAI motivation plus LLM-based platform features; EDUCON 2026 peer-reviewed conference; 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: System design and evaluation: distributed real-time keystroke-log anomaly detection (unsupervised Isolation Forest) with AST-normalised code-similarity search; synthetic load test plus an in-class evaluation with an honest control group and a group instructed to plagiarise
discipline: Computer science / programming (data structures and algorithms, competitive programming)
sample: Training data: 189 sophomore students in a 3-hour university hackathon (366,987 editing events). Evaluation: 101 sophomore students in a 2-hour in-class assignment (19 honest control, 82 instructed to plagiarise by any means)
genai_tools: LLMs inside the Superlit platform (constraint checking, hints, auto-generated code-specific verification questions; model not named); GraphCodeBERT embeddings with FAISS; Apache Kafka, Spark, Redis, Cassandra; Isolation Forest

key_findings.finding: Interface restrictions (full-screen, focus-change detection, paste limits) are easy to circumvent, so the system captures fine-grained editing logs and derives behavioural features (e.g. paste count, churn rate, deletion ratio, a Relative Jaggedness Index) to flag anomalous authorship processes.
key_findings.location: Sec II, Sec IV-B to IV-D, Tables I-II

key_findings.finding: In the in-class evaluation (N = 101), the system had 74 TP, 8 FN, 5 FP and 14 TN: accuracy 87.13%, precision 93.67%, recall 90.24%, F1 91.93%.
Students circumvented copy-paste restrictions as expected; about half of the true positives were manual transcription of AI-generated code, which process monitoring still detected.

False positives were honest students with heavy delete-and-rewrite styles. False negatives were late-stage plagiarism smoothed by earlier honest work; a mass-deletion baseline reset was added after the evaluation but not re-tested.
At submission, the platform also asks LLM-generated multiple-choice questions specific to the student's own code as an extra authorship check (not separately evaluated).

dimensions.capability_verification: Code-specific LLM-generated verification questions at submission are intended to check familiarity with the submitted code (not evaluated) (Sec III).
dimensions.integrity_security: Process-level behavioural monitoring detected most instructed plagiarism attempts, including transcription of AI code, which is presented as a complement or replacement for similarity checkers (Sec V-C, Sec VI).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: LLM hints guide students to the next conceptual step without giving full solutions (Sec III).
dimensions.scalability: Sustained 100 requests per second (each a batch of 150 logs) with 200 concurrent users at about 400 ms latency on 1-vCPU containers; designed for horizontal scaling (Sec V-A).
dimensions.workload: A dashboard with real-time alerts and code replay is meant to support instructor review (Sec IV-G).
dimensions.feasibility: Requires students to work in the custom Superlit web editor; future extensions to VS Code and browser plugins are proposed (Sec VI).
dimensions.process_visibility: Code replay reconstructs how a solution was developed over time and supports evidence-based integrity decisions (Sec IV-G).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Honest students with atypical iterative styles were falsely flagged; individualised baselines are proposed (Sec V-C, Sec VI).

author_recommendations: Use process-level activity-log monitoring as a complement to, or replacement for, similarity-based detectors (evaluated in one in-class deployment).
Build individualised behavioural baselines per student to reduce false positives (not tested).
Reset behavioural baselines after mass-deletion events to catch late-stage plagiarism (implemented after the evaluation; not tested).
Extend logging to VS Code and competitive-programming platforms, and add error-trajectory signals and an ensemble of models (not tested).
limitations: Authors discuss false positives and negatives and propose fixes (Sec V-C). Also noted: plagiarism was instructed rather than naturally occurring, with an imbalanced 82/19 split; ground truth was confirmed by invigilators using the system's own code-replay feature; single institution and single session; post-evaluation changes not re-tested; no discussion of student privacy, consent or surveillance ethics.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear contributions; samples well described; confusion matrix supports the reported metrics; limitations of detection discussed. q2 Unclear because the evaluation used instructed cheating with an imbalanced design and ground truth partly reliant on the system's own replay tool.

title: Redefining Undergraduate Computing Education with GenAI-Facilitated Authentic In-Term Assessment
authors: Anum Masood; Vindya Wijeratne; Atm S. Alam
venue: IEEE International Conference on Teaching, Assessment, and Learning for Engineering
ft_reason: Undergraduate programming module in transnational education; design of a GenAI-permitted assessment (prompt submission, reflection, individual viva) is a substantial focus; GenAI; IEEE TALE 2025 peer-reviewed conference; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Practice report / single-module case study: GenAI-permitted group mini-project assessed by report, code and individual viva; descriptive analysis of marks, student reflections and a usefulness survey; end-of-module quantitative survey pending
country: UK institution (Queen Mary University of London) delivering TNE programmes on two campuses in China
discipline: Introductory Java programming within BSc Engineering programmes (Digital Media Technology, Electronic Information Engineering, Intelligent Science and Technology, Telecommunications, IoT)
sample: Over 750 students across two TNE programmes, in self-formed groups (3-5 students); 8-week mini-project; numbers of reflections and survey respondents not reported
genai_tools: GenAI tools generally (ChatGPT discussed; specific tools used by students not reported)

key_findings.finding: GenAI was allowed for code generation, debugging, concepts and documentation (but not individual reflections); each group had to submit its three best prompts with justifications, and the reflection asked each student to describe their GenAI use.

Each student had a 10-minute individual viva in which they explained code and design decisions and responded to real-time modification requests; students in the same group with a well-written report sometimes received clearly different marks based on the viva.
Mark-review requests fell to around 10, which the authors describe as a substantial reduction from previous years (earlier figures not reported); they attribute this to clearer expectations.

Most students found GenAI helpful, but about 7% did not, and some students could not complete the project despite using GenAI; outcomes were not compared with earlier cohorts because the project was previously individual.
Claims that the design improved critical thinking and programming understanding are interpretive; the quantitative survey analysis was still pending.

dimensions.authenticity: Students built a Java GUI maths-learning tool for Key Stage 2-3 learners, with selected apps to be trialled by a partner school (Sec II-III, Sec IV).
dimensions.capability_verification: The individual viva with live code modifications was used to verify each student's contribution and understanding within group work (Sec III-B, Sec IV).
dimensions.integrity_security: Notes that unclear GenAI policies challenge academic integrity; the design relies on viva verification rather than detection (Sec IV).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Guidance gave acceptable and unacceptable prompt examples, and prompts were to support rather than outsource the task (Sec III-A).
dimensions.scalability: Implemented with over 750 students across two campuses using 10-minute individual vivas (Sec II).
dimensions.feasibility: Structured guidance and support were associated with consistent engagement across campuses in the TNE context (Sec IV).
dimensions.process_visibility: Submitted prompts with justifications and individual reflections expose part of the AI-assisted process (Sec III-A, Sec III-B).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Students were also required to design interfaces accessible to colour-blind children (Sec II).

author_recommendations: Combine permitted GenAI use with prompt submission, justification, reflection and an individual viva (implemented; evaluated only descriptively).
Extend the approach to other computing modules such as databases (not tested).
Teach AI literacy beyond technical skill, including fact-checking AI output and professional ethics (not tested).
limitations: Authors note no comparison with previous years and that the anonymous survey could not be linked to performance; quantitative survey analysis was pending (Sec IV). Also noted: no analysis method described for reflections; respondent numbers not reported; claims of improved critical thinking lack direct measures.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. RQs are stated, but data collection and analysis are only loosely described; the critical-thinking and understanding claims are not supported by data presented; some limitations are acknowledged.

title: A Framework for Assessment Design in the Era of Generative AI: Case Study of Take-Home Assignment in Software-related Courses
authors: Anna Lyza Felipe; Ushik Shrestha Khwakhali; Thanh Ngoc Nguyen
ft_reason: Undergraduate BIT/BSE courses at a university in Vietnam; take-home assessment design for integrity under GenAI is the primary focus; IEEE iSTEM-Ed 2025 conference framework paper; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Framework development from a small experiment: assessment questions from three courses classified by Bloom's level, entered into ChatGPT 3.5 (whole or broken down), outputs marked against the course rubrics, and a five-rule design framework derived
country: Vietnam (university anonymised as 'MUni'; author affiliations RMIT Vietnam); one author at University of Wollongong, Australia
discipline: Information technology / software engineering (BIT and BSE programmes)
sample: Three assessments from three courses: Advanced Programming Techniques (BSE year 3, group, 2 weeks, 35%), Enterprise Application Development (BSE year 2, individual, 3 days, 30%), Object-Oriented Programming (BIT year 1, individual final test, 2 hours, 40%); no student data

key_findings.finding: The three assessments were classified at Bloom's levels 3 (Applying) to 6 (Creating); ChatGPT outputs often had to be produced by breaking questions into parts and recombining answers.
key_findings.location: Sec IV-A, Sec IV-B, Table IV

key_findings.finding: Lecturers' rubric marking gave ChatGPT 3.5 'probable marks' of 70%, 65% and 75%, which the authors read as passing but short of outstanding performance.

The framework's five rules: prefer Bloom levels 5-6; use complex multi-part questions; include images; use invigilated in-class or online tests with screen recording and time limits; and require students to critique GenAI output.
The authors claim that following the framework will mitigate plagiarism, but the framework itself was not evaluated with students or new assessments.

dimensions.authenticity: Assessments required building fictional applications resembling real scenarios (delivery service, home sharing, quiz management) with complex features removed (Sec IV-A).
dimensions.capability_verification: Recommends invigilated time-limited tests with screen recording to verify independent capability (Sec IV-C, rule 4).
dimensions.integrity_security: ChatGPT 3.5 could reach 65-75% on the take-home tasks, motivating design rules to curb AI-enabled plagiarism (Sec IV-B, Table V).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Framework is built on aligning assessment with course learning objectives through Bloom's taxonomy levels (Sec II-C, Sec V).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Proposes integrating GenAI by requiring students to critique AI-generated answers (Sec IV-C, rule 5).
dimensions.feasibility: Notes some rules (e.g. images in questions) depend on current ChatGPT limits and will need updating for newer tools (Sec IV-C, Sec V).

author_recommendations: Set take-home questions at higher Bloom's levels, preferably 5-6 (not tested).
Use complex questions that cannot be answered by ChatGPT in one pass (not tested).
Include images in questions (not tested; tied to early ChatGPT versions).
Use invigilated in-class or online time-limited tests with screen recording (not tested).
Require students to critique GenAI outputs (not tested).
Re-test the framework with newer models (e.g. Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek) and other disciplines (future work).
limitations: No limitations section; only future work is stated (Sec V). Also noted: one model (ChatGPT 3.5) and three assessments; marks are 'probable' and marker numbers and process are not described, with an inconsistent statement that ChatGPT itself graded the answers (Sec III-A vs Sec IV-B); the abstract says Bloom levels 3-6 while rule 1 recommends levels 5-6; several rules are not derived from the results; one 'take-home' item was a 2-hour final test.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Aim is clear, but the experiment is small and thinly described; framework rules go beyond the data (e.g. images, invigilation) and are not evaluated; no limitations acknowledged.
